11	# 2.1 Simplicial and Singular Homology
12	
13	## $\Delta$-Complexes
14	
15	The torus, the projective plane, and the Klein bottle can each be obtained from a square by identifying opposite edges in the way indicated by arrows. Cutting a square along a diagonal produces two triangles, so each of these surfaces can also be built from two triangles by identifying their edges in pairs. In similar fashion a polygon with any number of sides can be cut along diagonals into triangles, so in fact all closed surfaces can be constructed from triangles by identifying edges. Thus we have a single building block, the triangle, from which all surfaces can be constructed. Using only triangles we could also construct a large class of 2-dimensional spaces that are not surfaces in the strict sense, by allowing more than two edges to be identified together at a time.
16	
17	The idea of a $\Delta$-complex is to generalize constructions like these to any number of dimensions. The $n$-dimensional analog of the triangle is the **$n$-simplex**. This is the smallest convex set in a Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^m$ containing $n+1$ points $v_0, \cdots, v_n$ that do not lie in a hyperplane of dimension less than $n$, where by a hyperplane we mean the set of solutions of a system of linear equations. An equivalent condition would be that the difference vectors $v_1 - v_0, \cdots, v_n - v_0$ are linearly independent. The points $v_i$ are the **vertices** of the simplex, and the simplex itself is denoted $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$. For example, there is the **standard $n$-simplex**
18	
19	$$
20	\Delta^n = \{(t_0, \cdots, t_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1} \mid \textstyle\sum_i t_i = 1 \text{ and } t_i \geq 0 \text{ for all } i\}
21	$$
22	
23	whose vertices are the unit vectors along the coordinate axes.
24	
25	For purposes of homology it will be important to keep track of the order of the vertices of a simplex, so '$n$-simplex' will really mean '$n$-simplex with an ordering of its vertices'. A by-product of ordering the vertices of a simplex $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$ is that this determines orientations of the edges $[v_i, v_j]$ according to increasing subscripts. Specifying the ordering of the vertices also determines a canonical linear homeomorphism from the standard $n$-simplex $\Delta^n$ onto any other $n$-simplex $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$, preserving the order of vertices, namely,
26	
27	$$
28	(t_0, \cdots, t_n) \longmapsto \textstyle\sum_i t_i v_i.
29	$$
30	
31	The coefficients $t_i$ are the **barycentric coordinates** of the point $\sum_i t_i v_i$ in $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$.
32	
33	If we delete one of the $n+1$ vertices of an $n$-simplex $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$, then the remaining $n$ vertices span an $(n-1)$-simplex, called a **face** of $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$. We adopt the following convention:
34	
35	> The vertices of a face, or of any subsimplex spanned by a subset of the vertices, will always be ordered according to their order in the larger simplex.
36	
37	The union of all the faces of $\Delta^n$ is the **boundary** of $\Delta^n$, written $\partial\Delta^n$. The **open simplex** $\mathring{\Delta}^n$ is $\Delta^n - \partial\Delta^n$, the interior of $\Delta^n$.
38	
39	A **$\Delta$-complex structure** on a space $X$ is a collection of maps $\sigma_\alpha : \Delta^n \to X$, with $n$ depending on the index $\alpha$, such that:
40	
41	1. The restriction $\sigma_\alpha \vert_{\mathring{\Delta}^n}$ is injective, and each point of $X$ is in the image of exactly one such restriction $\sigma_\alpha \vert_{\mathring{\Delta}^n}$.
42	2. Each restriction of $\sigma_\alpha$ to a face of $\Delta^n$ is one of the maps $\sigma_\beta : \Delta^{n-1} \to X$. Here we are identifying the face of $\Delta^n$ with $\Delta^{n-1}$ by the canonical linear homeomorphism between them that preserves the ordering of the vertices.
43	3. A set $A \subset X$ is open iff $\sigma_\alpha^{-1}(A)$ is open in $\Delta^n$ for each $\sigma_\alpha$.
44	
45	Among other things, this last condition rules out trivialities like regarding all the points of $X$ as individual vertices.
46	
47	A consequence of (3) is that $X$ can be built as a quotient space of a collection of disjoint simplices $\Delta^n_\alpha$, one for each $\sigma_\alpha : \Delta^n \to X$, the quotient space obtained by identifying each face of a $\Delta^n_\alpha$ with the $\Delta^{n-1}_\beta$ corresponding to the restriction $\sigma_\beta$ of $\sigma_\alpha$ to the face in question, as in condition (2). One can think of building the quotient space inductively, starting with a discrete set of vertices, then attaching edges to these to produce a graph, then attaching 2-simplices to the graph, and so on. From this viewpoint we see that the data specifying a $\Delta$-complex can be described purely combinatorially as collections of $n$-simplices $\sigma^n_\alpha$ for each $n$ together with functions associating to each face of each $n$-simplex $\sigma^n_\alpha$ an $(n-1)$-simplex $\sigma^{n-1}_\beta$.
48	
49	More generally, $\Delta$-complexes can be built from collections of disjoint simplices by identifying various subsimplices spanned by subsets of the vertices, where the identifications are performed using the canonical linear homeomorphisms that preserve the orderings of the vertices.
50	
51	Thinking of a $\Delta$-complex $X$ as a quotient space of a collection of disjoint simplices, it is not hard to see that $X$ must be a Hausdorff space. Condition (3) then implies that each restriction $\sigma_\alpha \vert_{\mathring{\Delta}^n}$ is a homeomorphism onto its image, which is thus an open simplex in $X$. It follows from Proposition A.2 in the Appendix that these open simplices $\sigma_\alpha(\mathring{\Delta}^n)$ are the cells $e^n_\alpha$ of a CW complex structure on $X$ with the $\sigma_\alpha$'s as characteristic maps.
52	
53	---
54	
55	## Simplicial Homology
56	
57	Our goal now is to define the simplicial homology groups of a $\Delta$-complex $X$. Let $\Delta_n(X)$ be the free abelian group with basis the open $n$-simplices $e^n_\alpha$ of $X$. Elements of $\Delta_n(X)$, called **$n$-chains**, can be written as finite formal sums $\sum_\alpha n_\alpha e^n_\alpha$ with coefficients $n_\alpha \in \mathbb{Z}$. Equivalently, we could write $\sum_\alpha n_\alpha \sigma_\alpha$ where $\sigma_\alpha : \Delta^n \to X$ is the characteristic map of $e^n_\alpha$. Such a sum $\sum_\alpha n_\alpha \sigma_\alpha$ can be thought of as a finite collection, or 'chain', of $n$-simplices in $X$ with integer multiplicities, the coefficients $n_\alpha$.
58	
59	The boundary of the $n$-simplex $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$ consists of the various $(n-1)$-dimensional simplices $[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n]$, where the 'hat' symbol $\hat{}$ over $v_i$ indicates that this vertex is deleted from the sequence $v_0, \cdots, v_n$. It turns out to be better to insert certain signs and let the boundary of $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$ be
60	
61	$$
62	\sum_i (-1)^i [v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n].
63	$$
64	
65	Heuristically, the signs are inserted to take orientations into account, so that all the faces of a simplex are coherently oriented:
66	
67	$$
68	\partial[v_0, v_1] = [v_1] - [v_0]
69	$$
70	
71	$$
72	\partial[v_0, v_1, v_2] = [v_1, v_2] - [v_0, v_2] + [v_0, v_1]
73	$$
74	
75	$$
76	\partial[v_0, v_1, v_2, v_3] = [v_1, v_2, v_3] - [v_0, v_2, v_3] + [v_0, v_1, v_3] - [v_0, v_1, v_2]
77	$$
78	
79	With this geometry in mind we define for a general $\Delta$-complex $X$ a **boundary homomorphism** $\partial_n : \Delta_n(X) \to \Delta_{n-1}(X)$ by specifying its values on basis elements:
80	
81	$$
82	\partial_n(\sigma_\alpha) = \sum_i (-1)^i \sigma_\alpha \vert_{[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n]}
83	$$
84	
85	Note that the right side of this equation does indeed lie in $\Delta_{n-1}(X)$ since each restriction $\sigma_\alpha \vert_{[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n]}$ is the characteristic map of an $(n-1)$-simplex of $X$.
86	
87	> [!theorem] Lemma 2.1
88	> The composition $\Delta_n(X) \xrightarrow{\partial_n} \Delta_{n-1}(X) \xrightarrow{\partial_{n-1}} \Delta_{n-2}(X)$ is zero.
89	
90	> [!proof]- Proof
91	> We have $\partial_n(\sigma_\alpha) = \sum_i (-1)^i \sigma_\alpha \vert_{[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n]}$, and hence
92	> $$\partial_{n-1}\partial_n(\sigma_\alpha) = \sum_{j<i} (-1)^i (-1)^j \sigma_\alpha \vert_{[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_j, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n]} + \sum_{j>i} (-1)^i (-1)^{j-1} \sigma_\alpha \vert_{[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, \hat{v}_j, \cdots, v_n]}$$
93	> The latter two summations cancel since after switching $i$ and $j$ in the second sum, it becomes the negative of the first. $\blacksquare$
94	
95	The algebraic situation we have now is a sequence of homomorphisms of abelian groups
96	
97	$$
98	\cdots \xrightarrow{} C_{n+1} \xrightarrow{\partial_{n+1}} C_n \xrightarrow{\partial_n} C_{n-1} \xrightarrow{} \cdots \xrightarrow{} C_1 \xrightarrow{\partial_1} C_0 \xrightarrow{\partial_0} 0
99	$$
100	
101	with $\partial_n \partial_{n+1} = 0$ for each $n$. Such a sequence is called a **chain complex**. Note that we have extended the sequence by a $0$ at the right end, with $\partial_0 = 0$. The equation $\partial_n \partial_{n+1} = 0$ is equivalent to the inclusion $\operatorname{Im} \partial_{n+1} \subset \operatorname{Ker} \partial_n$. So we can define the **$n$th homology group** of the chain complex to be the quotient group
102	
103	$$
104	H_n = \operatorname{Ker} \partial_n / \operatorname{Im} \partial_{n+1}.
105	$$
106	
107	Elements of $\operatorname{Ker} \partial_n$ are called **cycles** and elements of $\operatorname{Im} \partial_{n+1}$ are called **boundaries**. Elements of $H_n$ are cosets of $\operatorname{Im} \partial_{n+1}$, called **homology classes**. Two cycles representing the same homology class are said to be **homologous**. This means their difference is a boundary.
108	
109	Returning to the case that $C_n = \Delta_n(X)$, the homology group $\operatorname{Ker} \partial_n / \operatorname{Im} \partial_{n+1}$ will be denoted $H_n^\Delta(X)$ and called the **$n$th simplicial homology group** of $X$.
110	
111	> [!example] Example 2.2
112	> $X = S^1$, with one vertex $v$ and one edge $e$. Then $\Delta_0(S^1)$ and $\Delta_1(S^1)$ are both $\mathbb{Z}$ and the boundary map $\partial_1$ is zero since $\partial e = v - v$. The groups $\Delta_n(S^1)$ are $0$ for $n \geq 2$ since there are no simplices in these dimensions. Hence
113	> $$H_n^\Delta(S^1) \cong \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z} & \text{for } n = 0, 1 \\ 0 & \text{for } n \geq 2 \end{cases}$$
114	> This is an illustration of the general fact that if the boundary maps in a chain complex are all zero, then the homology groups of the complex are isomorphic to the chain groups themselves.
115	
116	> [!example] Example 2.3
117	> $X = T$, the torus with the $\Delta$-complex structure, having one vertex, three edges $a$, $b$, and $c$, and two 2-simplices $U$ and $L$. As in the previous example, $\partial_1 = 0$ so $H_0^\Delta(T) \cong \mathbb{Z}$. Since $\partial_2 U = a + b - c = \partial_2 L$ and $\{a, b, a+b-c\}$ is a basis for $\Delta_1(T)$, it follows that $H_1^\Delta(T) \cong \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}$ with basis the homology classes $[a]$ and $[b]$. Since there are no 3-simplices, $H_2^\Delta(T)$ is equal to $\operatorname{Ker} \partial_2$, which is infinite cyclic generated by $U - L$ since $\partial(pU + qL) = (p+q)(a+b-c) = 0$ only if $p = -q$. Thus
118	> $$H_n^\Delta(T) \cong \begin{cases} \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z} & \text{for } n = 1 \\ \mathbb{Z} & \text{for } n = 0, 2 \\ 0 & \text{for } n \geq 3 \end{cases}$$
119	
120	> [!example] Example 2.4
121	> $X = \mathbb{R}P^2$, with two vertices $v$ and $w$, three edges $a$, $b$, and $c$, and two 2-simplices $U$ and $L$. Then $\operatorname{Im} \partial_1$ is generated by $w - v$, so $H_0^\Delta(X) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ with either vertex as a generator. Since $\partial_2 U = -a + b + c$ and $\partial_2 L = a - b + c$, we see that $\partial_2$ is injective, so $H_2^\Delta(X) = 0$. Further, $\operatorname{Ker} \partial_1 \cong \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}$ with basis $a - b$ and $c$, and $\operatorname{Im} \partial_2$ is an index-two subgroup of $\operatorname{Ker} \partial_1$ since we can choose $c$ and $a - b + c$ as a basis for $\operatorname{Ker} \partial_1$ and $a - b + c$ and $2c = (a - b + c) + (-a + b + c)$ as a basis for $\operatorname{Im} \partial_2$. Thus $H_1^\Delta(X) \cong \mathbb{Z}_2$.
122	
123	> [!example] Example 2.5
124	> We can obtain a $\Delta$-complex structure on $S^n$ by taking two copies of $\Delta^n$ and identifying their boundaries via the identity map. Labeling these two $n$-simplices $U$ and $L$, then it is obvious that $\operatorname{Ker} \partial_n$ is infinite cyclic generated by $U - L$. Thus $H_n^\Delta(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ for this $\Delta$-complex structure on $S^n$.
125	
126	Many similar examples could be worked out without much trouble, such as the other closed orientable and nonorientable surfaces. However, the calculations do tend to increase in complexity before long, particularly for higher-dimensional complexes.
127	
128	Some obvious general questions arise: Are the groups $H_n^\Delta(X)$ independent of the choice of $\Delta$-complex structure on $X$? In other words, if two $\Delta$-complexes are homeomorphic, do they have isomorphic homology groups? More generally, do they have isomorphic homology groups if they are merely homotopy equivalent? To answer such questions and to develop a general theory it is best to leave the rather rigid simplicial realm and introduce the singular homology groups.
129	
130	---
131	
132	## Singular Homology
133	
134	A **singular $n$-simplex** in a space $X$ is by definition just a map $\sigma : \Delta^n \to X$. The word 'singular' is used here to express the idea that $\sigma$ need not be a nice embedding but can have 'singularities' where its image does not look at all like a simplex. All that is required is that $\sigma$ be continuous. Let $C_n(X)$ be the free abelian group with basis the set of singular $n$-simplices in $X$. Elements of $C_n(X)$, called **$n$-chains**, or more precisely **singular $n$-chains**, are finite formal sums $\sum_i n_i \sigma_i$ for $n_i \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $\sigma_i : \Delta^n \to X$.
135	
136	A boundary map $\partial_n : C_n(X) \to C_{n-1}(X)$ is defined by the same formula as before:
137	
138	$$
139	\partial_n(\sigma) = \sum_i (-1)^i \sigma \vert_{[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n]}
140	$$
141	
142	Implicit in this formula is the canonical identification of $[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n]$ with $\Delta^{n-1}$, preserving the ordering of vertices, so that $\sigma \vert_{[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n]}$ is regarded as a map $\Delta^{n-1} \to X$, that is, a singular $(n-1)$-simplex.
143	
144	Often we write the boundary map $\partial_n$ from $C_n(X)$ to $C_{n-1}(X)$ simply as $\partial$ when this does not lead to serious ambiguities. The proof of Lemma 2.1 applies equally well to singular simplices, showing that $\partial_n \partial_{n+1} = 0$ or more concisely $\partial^2 = 0$, so we can define the **singular homology group** $H_n(X) = \operatorname{Ker} \partial_n / \operatorname{Im} \partial_{n+1}$.
145	
146	It is evident from the definition that homeomorphic spaces have isomorphic singular homology groups $H_n$, in contrast with the situation for $H_n^\Delta$. On the other hand, since the groups $C_n(X)$ are so large, the number of singular $n$-simplices in $X$ usually being uncountable, it is not at all clear that for a $\Delta$-complex $X$ with finitely many simplices, $H_n(X)$ should be finitely generated for all $n$, or that $H_n(X)$ should be zero for $n$ larger than the dimension of $X$.
147	
148	Though singular homology looks so much more general than simplicial homology, it can actually be regarded as a special case of simplicial homology by means of the following construction. For an arbitrary space $X$, define the **singular complex** $S(X)$ to be the $\Delta$-complex with one $n$-simplex $\Delta^n_\sigma$ for each singular $n$-simplex $\sigma : \Delta^n \to X$, with $\Delta^n_\sigma$ attached in the obvious way to the $(n-1)$-simplices of $S(X)$ that are the restrictions of $\sigma$ to the various $(n-1)$-simplices in $\Delta^n$. It is clear from the definitions that $H_n^\Delta(S(X))$ is identical with $H_n(X)$ for all $n$, and in this sense the singular homology group $H_n(X)$ is a special case of a simplicial homology group.
149	
150	> [!remark]
151	> Cycles in singular homology are defined algebraically, but they can be given a somewhat more geometric interpretation in terms of maps from finite $\Delta$-complexes. In particular, elements of $H_1(X)$ are represented by collections of oriented loops in $X$, and elements of $H_2(X)$ are represented by maps of closed oriented surfaces into $X$.
152	
153	> [!proposition] Proposition 2.6
154	> Corresponding to the decomposition of a space $X$ into its path-components $X_\alpha$ there is an isomorphism of $H_n(X)$ with the direct sum $\bigoplus_\alpha H_n(X_\alpha)$.
155	
156	> [!proof]- Proof
157	> Since a singular simplex always has path-connected image, $C_n(X)$ splits as the direct sum of its subgroups $C_n(X_\alpha)$. The boundary maps $\partial_n$ preserve this direct sum decomposition, taking $C_n(X_\alpha)$ to $C_{n-1}(X_\alpha)$, so $\operatorname{Ker} \partial_n$ and $\operatorname{Im} \partial_{n+1}$ split similarly as direct sums, hence the homology groups also split, $H_n(X) \cong \bigoplus_\alpha H_n(X_\alpha)$. $\blacksquare$
158	
159	> [!proposition] Proposition 2.7
160	> If $X$ is nonempty and path-connected, then $H_0(X) \cong \mathbb{Z}$. Hence for any space $X$, $H_0(X)$ is a direct sum of $\mathbb{Z}$'s, one for each path-component of $X$.
161	
162	> [!proof]- Proof
163	> By definition, $H_0(X) = C_0(X)/\operatorname{Im} \partial_1$ since $\partial_0 = 0$. Define a homomorphism $\varepsilon : C_0(X) \to \mathbb{Z}$ by $\varepsilon(\sum_i n_i \sigma_i) = \sum_i n_i$. This is obviously surjective if $X$ is nonempty. The claim is that $\operatorname{Ker} \varepsilon = \operatorname{Im} \partial_1$ if $X$ is path-connected, and hence $\varepsilon$ induces an isomorphism $H_0(X) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.
164	>
165	> To verify the claim, observe first that $\operatorname{Im} \partial_1 \subset \operatorname{Ker} \varepsilon$ since for a singular 1-simplex $\sigma : \Delta^1 \to X$ we have $\varepsilon(\partial_1(\sigma)) = \varepsilon(\sigma\vert_{[v_1]} - \sigma\vert_{[v_0]}) = 1 - 1 = 0$. For the reverse inclusion $\operatorname{Ker} \varepsilon \subset \operatorname{Im} \partial_1$, suppose $\sum_i n_i \sigma_i$ satisfies $\sum_i n_i = 0$. The $\sigma_i$'s are singular 0-simplices, which are simply points of $X$. Choose a path $\tau_i : I \to X$ from a basepoint $x_0$ to $\sigma_i(v_0)$ and let $\sigma_0$ be the singular 0-simplex with image $x_0$. We can view $\tau_i$ as a singular 1-simplex, and then we have $\partial \tau_i = \sigma_i - \sigma_0$. Hence $\sum_i n_i \sigma_i = \sum_i n_i \partial \tau_i - \sum_i n_i \sigma_0 = \sum_i n_i \partial \tau_i$ since $\sum_i n_i = 0$. Thus $\sum_i n_i \sigma_i$ is a boundary. $\blacksquare$
166	
167	> [!proposition] Proposition 2.8
168	> If $X$ is a point, then $H_n(X) = 0$ for $n > 0$ and $H_0(X) \cong \mathbb{Z}$.
169	
170	> [!proof]- Proof
171	> In this case there is a unique singular $n$-simplex $\sigma_n$ for each $n$, and $\partial(\sigma_n) = \sum_i (-1)^i \sigma_{n-1}$, a sum of $n+1$ terms, which is therefore $0$ for $n$ odd and $\sigma_{n-1}$ for $n$ even, $n \geq 0$. Thus we have the chain complex
172	> $$\cdots \to \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{\cong} \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{0} \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{\cong} \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{0} \mathbb{Z} \to 0$$
173	> with boundary maps alternately isomorphisms and trivial maps, except at the last $\mathbb{Z}$. The homology groups of this complex are trivial except for $H_0 \cong \mathbb{Z}$. $\blacksquare$
174	
175	### Reduced Homology
176	
177	It is often very convenient to have a slightly modified version of homology for which a point has trivial homology groups in all dimensions, including zero. This is done by defining the **reduced homology groups** $\widetilde{H}_n(X)$ to be the homology groups of the **augmented chain complex**
178	
179	$$
180	\cdots \to C_2(X) \xrightarrow{\partial_2} C_1(X) \xrightarrow{\partial_1} C_0(X) \xrightarrow{\varepsilon} \mathbb{Z} \to 0
181	$$
182	
183	where $\varepsilon(\sum_i n_i \sigma_i) = \sum_i n_i$ as in the proof of Proposition 2.7. Here we had better require $X$ to be nonempty, to avoid having a nontrivial homology group in dimension $-1$. Since $\varepsilon \partial_1 = 0$, $\varepsilon$ vanishes on $\operatorname{Im} \partial_1$ and hence induces a map $H_0(X) \to \mathbb{Z}$ with kernel $\widetilde{H}_0(X)$, so $H_0(X) \cong \widetilde{H}_0(X) \oplus \mathbb{Z}$. Obviously $\widetilde{H}_n(X) \cong H_n(X)$ for $n > 0$.
184	
185	Formally, one can think of the extra $\mathbb{Z}$ in the augmented chain complex as generated by the unique map $[\,] \to X$ where $[\,]$ is the empty simplex, with no vertices. The augmentation map $\varepsilon$ is then the usual boundary map since $\partial[v_0] = \partial([v_0]) = [\,]$.

189	## Homotopy Invariance
190	
191	The first substantial result we will prove about singular homology is that homotopy equivalent spaces have isomorphic homology groups. This will be done by showing that a map $f : X \to Y$ induces a homomorphism $f_* : H_n(X) \to H_n(Y)$ for each $n$, and that $f_*$ is an isomorphism if $f$ is a homotopy equivalence.
192	
193	For a map $f : X \to Y$, an induced homomorphism $f_\# : C_n(X) \to C_n(Y)$ is defined by composing each singular $n$-simplex $\sigma : \Delta^n \to X$ with $f$ to get a singular $n$-simplex $f_\#(\sigma) = f \circ \sigma : \Delta^n \to Y$, then extending $f_\#$ linearly via $f_\#(\sum_i n_i \sigma_i) = \sum_i n_i f_\#(\sigma_i)$.
194	
195	The maps $f_\# : C_n(X) \to C_n(Y)$ satisfy $f_\# \partial = \partial f_\#$ since
196	
197	$$
198	f_\#(\partial \sigma) = f_\# \sum_i (-1)^i \sigma\vert_{[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n]} = \sum_i (-1)^i f \circ \sigma\vert_{[v_0, \cdots, \hat{v}_i, \cdots, v_n]} = \partial(f_\#(\sigma))
199	$$
200	
201	The fact that the maps $f_\# : C_n(X) \to C_n(Y)$ satisfy $f_\# \partial = \partial f_\#$ is also expressed by saying that the $f_\#$'s define a **chain map** from the singular chain complex of $X$ to that of $Y$. The relation $f_\# \partial = \partial f_\#$ implies that $f_\#$ takes cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries. Hence $f_\#$ induces a homomorphism $f_* : H_n(X) \to H_n(Y)$.
202	
203	> [!proposition] Proposition 2.9
204	> A chain map between chain complexes induces homomorphisms between the homology groups of the two complexes.
205	
206	Two basic properties of induced homomorphisms:
207	
208	1. $(fg)_* = f_* g_*$ for a composed mapping $X \xrightarrow{g} Y \xrightarrow{f} Z$.
209	2. $\mathbb{1}_* = \mathbb{1}$ where $\mathbb{1}$ denotes the identity map of a space or a group.
210	
211	> [!theorem] Theorem 2.10
212	> If two maps $f, g : X \to Y$ are homotopic, then they induce the same homomorphism $f_* = g_* : H_n(X) \to H_n(Y)$.
213

215	> The maps $f_* : H_n(X) \to H_n(Y)$ induced by a homotopy equivalence $f : X \to Y$ are isomorphisms for all $n$.

217	For example, if $X$ is contractible then $H_n(X) = 0$ for all $n$.

219	> [!proof]- Proof of Theorem 2.10
220	> The essential ingredient is a procedure for subdividing $\Delta^n \times I$ into simplices. In $\Delta^n \times I$, let $\Delta^n \times \{0\} = [v_0, \cdots, v_n]$ and $\Delta^n \times \{1\} = [w_0, \cdots, w_n]$, where $v_i$ and $w_i$ have the same image under the projection $\Delta^n \times I \to \Delta^n$. We can pass from $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$ to $[w_0, \cdots, w_n]$ by interpolating a sequence of $n$-simplices, each obtained from the preceding one by moving one vertex $v_i$ up to $w_i$, starting with $v_n$ and working backwards to $v_0$. The region between two consecutive $n$-simplices is exactly the $(n+1)$-simplex $[v_0, \cdots, v_i, w_i, \cdots, w_n]$. Altogether, $\Delta^n \times I$ is the union of the $(n+1)$-simplices $[v_0, \cdots, v_i, w_i, \cdots, w_n]$, each intersecting the next in an $n$-simplex face.
221	>
222	> Given a homotopy $F : X \times I \to Y$ from $f$ to $g$ and a singular simplex $\sigma : \Delta^n \to X$, we can form the composition $F \circ (\sigma \times \mathbb{1}) : \Delta^n \times I \to X \times I \to Y$. Using this, we define **prism operators** $P : C_n(X) \to C_{n+1}(Y)$ by:
223	> $$P(\sigma) = \sum_i (-1)^i F \circ (\sigma \times \mathbb{1})\vert_{[v_0, \cdots, v_i, w_i, \cdots, w_n]}$$
224	>
225	> These prism operators satisfy the basic relation:
226	> $$\partial P = g_\# - f_\# - P\partial$$
227	>
228	> Geometrically, the left side represents the boundary of the prism, and the three terms on the right side represent the top $\Delta^n \times \{1\}$, the bottom $\Delta^n \times \{0\}$, and the sides $\partial\Delta^n \times I$ of the prism.
229	>
230	> Now we can finish the proof. If $\alpha \in C_n(X)$ is a cycle, then $g_\#(\alpha) - f_\#(\alpha) = \partial P(\alpha) + P(\partial\alpha) = \partial P(\alpha)$ since $\partial\alpha = 0$. Thus $g_\#(\alpha) - f_\#(\alpha)$ is a boundary, so $g_\#(\alpha)$ and $f_\#(\alpha)$ determine the same homology class, which means that $g_*$ equals $f_*$ on the homology class of $\alpha$. $\blacksquare$
231	
232	The relationship $\partial P + P\partial = g_\# - f_\#$ is expressed by saying $P$ is a **chain homotopy** between the chain maps $f_\#$ and $g_\#$.
233

235	> Chain-homotopic chain maps induce the same homomorphism on homology.

241	## Exact Sequences and Excision
242	
243	If there was always a simple relationship between the homology groups of a space $X$, a subspace $A$, and the quotient space $X/A$, then this could be a very useful tool. Perhaps the simplest possible relationship would be if $H_n(X)$ contained $H_n(A)$ as a subgroup and the quotient group $H_n(X)/H_n(A)$ was isomorphic to $H_n(X/A)$. While this does hold in some cases, if it held in general then homology theory would collapse totally since every space $X$ can be embedded as a subspace of a space with trivial homology groups, namely the cone $CX = (X \times I)/(X \times \{0\})$, which is contractible.
244	
245	A sequence of homomorphisms
246	
247	$$
248	\cdots \xrightarrow{} A_{n+1} \xrightarrow{\alpha_{n+1}} A_n \xrightarrow{\alpha_n} A_{n-1} \xrightarrow{} \cdots
249	$$
250	
251	is said to be **exact** if $\operatorname{Ker} \alpha_n = \operatorname{Im} \alpha_{n+1}$ for each $n$. The inclusions $\operatorname{Im} \alpha_{n+1} \subset \operatorname{Ker} \alpha_n$ are equivalent to $\alpha_n \alpha_{n+1} = 0$, so the sequence is a chain complex, and the opposite inclusions $\operatorname{Ker} \alpha_n \subset \operatorname{Im} \alpha_{n+1}$ say that the homology groups of this chain complex are trivial.
252	
253	A number of basic algebraic concepts can be expressed in terms of exact sequences:
254	
255	1. $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\alpha} B$ is exact iff $\operatorname{Ker} \alpha = 0$, i.e., $\alpha$ is injective.
256	2. $A \xrightarrow{\alpha} B \to 0$ is exact iff $\operatorname{Im} \alpha = B$, i.e., $\alpha$ is surjective.
257	3. $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\alpha} B \to 0$ is exact iff $\alpha$ is an isomorphism, by (1) and (2).
258	4. $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\alpha} B \xrightarrow{\beta} C \to 0$ is exact iff $\alpha$ is injective, $\beta$ is surjective, and $\operatorname{Ker} \beta = \operatorname{Im} \alpha$, so $\beta$ induces an isomorphism $C \cong B/\operatorname{Im} \alpha$.
259	
260	An exact sequence $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$ as in (4) is called a **short exact sequence**.
261	
262	> [!theorem] Theorem 2.13
263	> If $X$ is a space and $A$ is a nonempty closed subspace that is a deformation retract of some neighborhood in $X$, then there is an exact sequence
264	> $$\cdots \to \widetilde{H}_n(A) \xrightarrow{i_*} \widetilde{H}_n(X) \xrightarrow{j_*} \widetilde{H}_n(X/A) \xrightarrow{\partial} \widetilde{H}_{n-1}(A) \xrightarrow{i_*} \widetilde{H}_{n-1}(X) \to \cdots$$
265	> $$\cdots \to \widetilde{H}_0(X/A) \to 0$$
266	> where $i$ is the inclusion $A \hookrightarrow X$ and $j$ is the quotient map $X \to X/A$.
267	
268	The map $\partial$ will be constructed in the course of the proof. The idea is that an element $x \in \widetilde{H}_n(X/A)$ can be represented by a chain $\alpha$ in $X$ with $\partial\alpha$ a cycle in $A$ whose homology class is $\partial x \in \widetilde{H}_{n-1}(A)$.
269	
270	Pairs of spaces $(X, A)$ satisfying the hypothesis of the theorem will be called **good pairs**. For example, if $X$ is a CW complex and $A$ is a nonempty subcomplex, then $(X, A)$ is a good pair by Proposition A.5 in the Appendix.
271	
272	> [!corollary] Corollary 2.14
273	> $\widetilde{H}_n(S^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and $\widetilde{H}_i(S^n) = 0$ for $i \neq n$.
274	
275	> [!proof]- Proof
276	> For $n > 0$ take $(X, A) = (D^n, S^{n-1})$ so $X/A = S^n$. The terms $\widetilde{H}_i(D^n)$ in the long exact sequence for this pair are zero since $D^n$ is contractible. Exactness of the sequence then implies that the maps $\widetilde{H}_i(S^n) \xrightarrow{\partial} \widetilde{H}_{i-1}(S^{n-1})$ are isomorphisms for $i > 0$ and that $\widetilde{H}_0(S^n) = 0$. The result now follows by induction on $n$, starting with the case of $S^0$ where the result holds by Propositions 2.6 and 2.8. $\blacksquare$
277	
278	> [!corollary] Corollary 2.15 (Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem)
279	> $\partial D^n$ is not a retract of $D^n$. Hence every map $f : D^n \to D^n$ has a fixed point.

281	> [!proof]- Proof
282	> If $r : D^n \to \partial D^n$ is a retraction, then $r \circ i = \mathbb{1}$ for $i : \partial D^n \hookrightarrow D^n$ the inclusion map. The composition $H_{n-1}(\partial D^n) \xrightarrow{i_*} H_{n-1}(D^n) \xrightarrow{r_*} H_{n-1}(\partial D^n)$ is then the identity map on $H_{n-1}(\partial D^n) \cong \mathbb{Z}$. But $i_*$ and $r_*$ are both $0$ since $H_{n-1}(D^n) = 0$, and we have a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

284	### Relative Homology Groups
285	
286	Relative homology groups are defined in the following way. Given a space $X$ and a subspace $A \subset X$, let $C_n(X, A)$ be the quotient group $C_n(X)/C_n(A)$. Thus chains in $A$ are trivial in $C_n(X, A)$. Since the boundary map $\partial : C_n(X) \to C_{n-1}(X)$ takes $C_n(A)$ to $C_{n-1}(A)$, it induces a quotient boundary map $\partial : C_n(X, A) \to C_{n-1}(X, A)$. The relation $\partial^2 = 0$ holds for these boundary maps since it holds before passing to quotient groups. So we have a chain complex, and the homology groups $\operatorname{Ker} \partial / \operatorname{Im} \partial$ of this chain complex are by definition the **relative homology groups** $H_n(X, A)$.
287	
288	Elements of $H_n(X, A)$ are represented by **relative cycles**: $n$-chains $\alpha \in C_n(X)$ such that $\partial\alpha \in C_{n-1}(A)$. A relative cycle $\alpha$ is trivial in $H_n(X, A)$ iff it is a **relative boundary**: $\alpha = \partial\beta + \gamma$ for some $\beta \in C_{n+1}(X)$ and $\gamma \in C_n(A)$.
289	
290	The relative homology groups $H_n(X, A)$ for any pair $(X, A)$ fit into a **long exact sequence**:
291	
292	$$
293	\cdots \to H_n(A) \xrightarrow{i_*} H_n(X) \xrightarrow{j_*} H_n(X, A) \xrightarrow{\partial} H_{n-1}(A) \xrightarrow{i_*} H_{n-1}(X) \to \cdots \to H_0(X, A) \to 0
294	$$
295	
296	This will be entirely a matter of algebra. Consider the diagram of short exact sequences $0 \to C_n(A) \xrightarrow{i} C_n(X) \xrightarrow{j} C_n(X, A) \to 0$ where $i$ is inclusion and $j$ is the quotient map. Letting $n$ vary, we have a **short exact sequence of chain complexes**. We will show that when we pass to homology groups, this short exact sequence of chain complexes stretches out into a long exact sequence of homology groups.
297	
298	> [!theorem] Theorem 2.16
299	> The sequence of homology groups
300	> $$\cdots \to H_n(A) \xrightarrow{i_*} H_n(B) \xrightarrow{j_*} H_n(C) \xrightarrow{\partial} H_{n-1}(A) \xrightarrow{i_*} H_{n-1}(B) \to \cdots$$
301	> is exact.
302	
303	> [!proof]- Proof
304	> There are six things to verify:
305	>
306	> **$\operatorname{Im} i_* \subset \operatorname{Ker} j_*$:** This is immediate since $ji = 0$ implies $j_* i_* = 0$.
307	>
308	> **$\operatorname{Im} j_* \subset \operatorname{Ker} \partial$:** We have $j_*\partial = 0$ since in this case $\partial b = 0$ in the definition of $\partial$.
309	>
310	> **$\operatorname{Im} \partial \subset \operatorname{Ker} i_*$:** Here $i_*\partial = 0$ since $i_*$ takes $[c]$ to $[\partial b] = 0$.
311	>
312	> **$\operatorname{Ker} j_* \subset \operatorname{Im} i_*$:** A homology class in $\operatorname{Ker} j_*$ is represented by a cycle $b \in B_n$ with $j(b)$ a boundary, so $j(b) = \partial c'$ for some $c' \in C_{n+1}$. Since $j$ is surjective, $c' = j(b')$ for some $b' \in B_{n+1}$. We have $j(b - \partial b') = j(b) - j(\partial b') = j(b) - \partial j(b') = 0$. So $b - \partial b' = i(a)$ for some $a \in A_n$. This $a$ is a cycle since $i(\partial a) = \partial i(a) = \partial(b - \partial b') = \partial b = 0$ and $i$ is injective. Thus $i_*[a] = [b - \partial b'] = [b]$.
313	>
314	> **$\operatorname{Ker} \partial \subset \operatorname{Im} j_*$:** If $c$ represents a class in $\operatorname{Ker} \partial$, then $a = \partial a'$ for some $a' \in A_n$. The element $b - i(a')$ is a cycle since $\partial(b - i(a')) = \partial b - i(\partial a') = \partial b - i(a) = 0$. And $j(b - i(a')) = j(b) - ji(a') = j(b) = c$, so $j_*$ maps $[b - i(a')]$ to $[c]$.
315	>
316	> **$\operatorname{Ker} i_* \subset \operatorname{Im} \partial$:** Given a cycle $a \in A_{n-1}$ such that $i(a) = \partial b$ for some $b \in B_n$, then $j(b)$ is a cycle since $\partial j(b) = j(\partial b) = ji(a) = 0$, and $\partial$ takes $[j(b)]$ to $[a]$. $\blacksquare$

318	This theorem represents the beginnings of the subject of **homological algebra**. The method of proof is sometimes called **diagram chasing**.

340	### Excision
341	
342	A fundamental property of relative homology groups is given by the following Excision Theorem, describing when the relative groups $H_n(X, A)$ are unaffected by deleting, or excising, a subset $Z \subset A$.
343	
344	> [!theorem] Theorem 2.20 (Excision)
345	> Given subspaces $Z \subset A \subset X$ such that the closure of $Z$ is contained in the interior of $A$, then the inclusion $(X - Z, A - Z) \hookrightarrow (X, A)$ induces isomorphisms $H_n(X - Z, A - Z) \to H_n(X, A)$ for all $n$.
346	>
347	> Equivalently, for subspaces $A, B \subset X$ whose interiors cover $X$, the inclusion $(B, A \cap B) \hookrightarrow (X, A)$ induces isomorphisms $H_n(B, A \cap B) \to H_n(X, A)$ for all $n$.
348	
349	The translation between the two versions is obtained by setting $B = X - Z$ and $Z = X - B$. Then $A \cap B = A - Z$ and the condition $\overline{Z} \subset \operatorname{int} A$ is equivalent to $X = \operatorname{int} A \cup \operatorname{int} B$ since $X - \operatorname{int} B = \overline{Z}$.
350	
351	The proof of the excision theorem involves a rather lengthy technical detour involving a construction known as **barycentric subdivision**, which allows homology groups to be computed using small singular simplices.
352	
353	> [!proposition] Proposition 2.21
354	> For a space $X$ with a collection $\mathcal{U} = \{U_j\}$ of subspaces whose interiors form an open cover of $X$, let $C_n^{\mathcal{U}}(X)$ be the subgroup of $C_n(X)$ consisting of chains $\sum_i n_i \sigma_i$ such that each $\sigma_i$ has image contained in some set in the cover $\mathcal{U}$. The inclusion $\iota : C_n^{\mathcal{U}}(X) \hookrightarrow C_n(X)$ is a chain homotopy equivalence, and hence $\iota$ induces isomorphisms $H_n^{\mathcal{U}}(X) \cong H_n(X)$ for all $n$.
355	
356	> [!proof]- Proof (Sketch)
357	> The proof proceeds in four stages:
358	>
359	> **(1) Barycentric Subdivision of Simplices.** The barycenter of $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$ is the point $b = \sum_i t_i v_i$ with $t_i = 1/(n+1)$ for each $i$. The barycentric subdivision of $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$ is defined inductively: it is the decomposition into $n$-simplices $[b, w_0, \cdots, w_{n-1}]$ where $[w_0, \cdots, w_{n-1}]$ is an $(n-1)$-simplex in the barycentric subdivision of a face. A key fact: the diameter of each simplex of the barycentric subdivision is at most $\frac{n}{n+1}$ times the diameter of $[v_0, \cdots, v_n]$.
360	>
361	> **(2) Barycentric Subdivision of Linear Chains.** For a convex set $Y$, define a subdivision homomorphism $S : LC_n(Y) \to LC_n(Y)$ inductively by $S(\lambda) = b_\lambda(S(\partial\lambda))$ where $b_\lambda$ is the cone operator. One shows $\partial S = S\partial$ and constructs a chain homotopy $T : LC_n(Y) \to LC_{n+1}(Y)$ between $S$ and the identity satisfying $\partial T + T\partial = \mathbb{1} - S$.
362	>
363	> **(3) Barycentric Subdivision of General Chains.** Define $S : C_n(X) \to C_n(X)$ by $S(\sigma) = \sigma_\#(S(\Delta^n))$ and $T : C_n(X) \to C_{n+1}(X)$ by $T(\sigma) = \sigma_\#(T(\Delta^n))$. These satisfy $\partial S = S\partial$ and $\partial T + T\partial = \mathbb{1} - S$.
364	>
365	> **(4) Iterated Barycentric Subdivision.** A chain homotopy between $\mathbb{1}$ and $S^m$ is given by $D_m = \sum_{0 \leq i < m} T S^i$. For each singular $n$-simplex $\sigma$, there exists an $m$ such that $S^m(\sigma)$ lies in $C_n^{\mathcal{U}}(X)$. Using this, one constructs a chain map $\rho : C_n(X) \to C_n^{\mathcal{U}}(X)$ that is a chain homotopy inverse for $\iota$. $\blacksquare$

395	> [!theorem] Theorem 2.26 (Invariance of Dimension)
396	> If nonempty open sets $U \subset \mathbb{R}^m$ and $V \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ are homeomorphic, then $m = n$.
397	
398	> [!proof]- Proof
399	> For $x \in U$ we have $H_k(U, U - \{x\}) \cong H_k(\mathbb{R}^m, \mathbb{R}^m - \{x\})$ by excision. From the long exact sequence for the pair $(\mathbb{R}^m, \mathbb{R}^m - \{x\})$ we get $H_k(\mathbb{R}^m, \mathbb{R}^m - \{x\}) \cong \widetilde{H}_{k-1}(\mathbb{R}^m - \{x\})$. Since $\mathbb{R}^m - \{x\}$ deformation retracts onto a sphere $S^{m-1}$, we conclude that $H_k(U, U - \{x\})$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ for $k = m$ and $0$ otherwise. By the same reasoning, $H_k(V, V - \{y\})$ is $\mathbb{Z}$ for $k = n$ and $0$ otherwise. Since a homeomorphism $h : U \to V$ induces isomorphisms $H_k(U, U - \{x\}) \to H_k(V, V - \{h(x)\})$ for all $k$, we must have $m = n$. $\blacksquare$
400	
401	Generalizing the idea of this proof, the **local homology groups** of a space $X$ at a point $x \in X$ are defined to be the groups $H_n(X, X - \{x\})$. For any open neighborhood $U$ of $x$, excision gives isomorphisms $H_n(X, X - \{x\}) \cong H_n(U, U - \{x\})$, and thus the groups $H_n(X, X - \{x\})$ depend only on the local topology of $X$ near $x$.
402	
403	### Naturality
404	
405	The exact sequences we have been constructing have an extra property called **naturality**. For example, to say that the long exact sequence of a pair is natural means that for a map $f : (X, A) \to (Y, B)$, the diagram
406	
407	$$
408	\begin{CD}
409	\cdots @>>> H_n(A) @>{i_*}>> H_n(X) @>{j_*}>> H_n(X,A) @>{\partial}>> H_{n-1}(A) @>>> \cdots \\
410	@. @V{f_*}VV @V{f_*}VV @V{f_*}VV @V{f_*}VV \\
411	\cdots @>>> H_n(B) @>{i_*}>> H_n(Y) @>{j_*}>> H_n(Y,B) @>{\partial}>> H_{n-1}(B) @>>> \cdots
412	\end{CD}
413	$$
414	
415	is commutative. This follows from the general algebraic fact that the long exact sequence of homology groups associated to a short exact sequence of chain complexes is natural.
416	
417	---
418	
419	## The Equivalence of Simplicial and Singular Homology
420	
421	We can use the preceding results to show that the simplicial and singular homology groups of $\Delta$-complexes are always isomorphic.
422	
423	> [!theorem] Theorem 2.27
424	> The homomorphisms $H_n^\Delta(X, A) \to H_n(X, A)$ are isomorphisms for all $n$ and all $\Delta$-complex pairs $(X, A)$.
425	
426	> [!proof]- Proof (Sketch)
427	> **Finite-dimensional case, $A = \varnothing$:** For $X^k$ the $k$-skeleton of $X$, we have a commutative diagram of exact sequences. The maps $H_n^\Delta(X^k, X^{k-1}) \to H_n(X^k, X^{k-1})$ are isomorphisms since $X^k/X^{k-1}$ is a wedge of $k$-spheres. By induction on $k$ and the **Five-Lemma**, the middle vertical map is an isomorphism.
428	>
429	> **The Five-Lemma:** In a commutative diagram of abelian groups with exact rows, if $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\delta$, and $\varepsilon$ are isomorphisms, then $\gamma$ is an isomorphism also. It suffices to show:
430	> - (a) $\gamma$ is surjective if $\beta$ and $\delta$ are surjective and $\varepsilon$ is injective.
431	> - (b) $\gamma$ is injective if $\beta$ and $\delta$ are injective and $\alpha$ is surjective.
432	>
433	> **Infinite-dimensional case:** A compact set in $X$ can meet only finitely many open simplices of $X$. This is used to show surjectivity and injectivity of $H_n^\Delta(X) \to H_n(X)$ by reducing to the finite-dimensional case.
434	>
435	> **Relative case:** Follows from the absolute case by applying the five-lemma to the canonical map from the long exact sequence of simplicial homology to the corresponding long exact sequence of singular homology. $\blacksquare$
436	
437	We can deduce from this theorem that $H_n(X)$ is finitely generated whenever $X$ is a $\Delta$-complex with finitely many $n$-simplices, since in this case the simplicial chain group $\Delta_n(X)$ is finitely generated, hence also its subgroup of cycles and therefore also the latter group's quotient $H_n^\Delta(X)$.
438	
439	If we write $H_n(X)$ as the direct sum of cyclic groups, then the number of $\mathbb{Z}$ summands is known traditionally as the **$n$th Betti number** of $X$, and integers specifying the orders of the finite cyclic summands are called **torsion coefficients**.
